Short story collection by Argentine writer [[Jorge Luis Borges]].

*Ficciones* ("Fictions") was written and published in Spanish between 1941 and 1956. Its first part, *The Garden of Forking Paths*, gathered eight stories from a 1941 volume; a second part, "Artifices," of six stories was added in 1944, and Borges added three more to it in the 1956 edition. Recurring motifs include the labyrinth, invented worlds, infinite libraries and paradoxical authorship, as in "Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius" and "The Library of Babel." The book became Borges's best-known work and made him known worldwide. Its English edition, published by Grove Press in 1962, was edited by Anthony Kerrigan.

Internally consistent fictional setting used in a narrative or work of art.

Also called an imagined universe, constructed universe or diegetic world, the concept is most associated with [[Fantasy|fantasy]] and [[Science fiction|science fiction]] works, appearing in novels, [[Comics|comics]], films, [[Television show|television shows]] and [[Video game|video games]]. In science fiction, a universe may be a remote alien planet or galaxy with little apparent relationship to the real world, as in [[Star Wars]]. In fantasy, it may be a greatly fictionalized or invented version of Earth's distant past or future, as in [[The Lord of the Rings]].

Comics historian Don Markstein proposed in 1970 that characters who meet in a story share a universe, a definition based on continuity. Some universes are shared by several authors: Larry Niven's Known Space allows other writers to contribute stories about the Man-Kzin Wars across an approximately 135-year period.

Species of [[Fig|fig]] tree also called the sycamore fig or fig-mulberry, because its leaves resemble those of the mulberry.

Native to [[Africa]] south of the Sahel and north of the Tropic of Capricorn, excluding central-west rainforest areas, *Ficus sycomorus* also grows in [[Lebanon]], the southern Arabian Peninsula, [[Cyprus]], very localized areas of [[Madagascar]], Palestine and [[Egypt]]. It is a protected tree in Israel, where it provides shade despite its roots cracking walls and pipes. The tree grows to 20 meters (66 ft) tall with a dense, round crown, and its large edible figs ripen from buff-green to yellow or red, borne in clusters on branchlets or the leaf axil.

Botanists Daniel Zohary and Maria Hopf note that the [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]] cultivated the species almost exclusively. Its remains appear in predynastic times and in quantity from the start of the third millennium BC, and it was the ancient Egyptian tree of life.

Musical with music by Jerry Bock, lyrics by Sheldon Harnick and book by Joseph Stein, based on stories by Sholem Aleichem written in [[Yiddish]].

Set in the fictional village of Anatevka in Imperial Russia in or around 1905, it follows the milkman Tevye as his three older daughters seek to marry for love. The original Broadway production, which opened in 1964, ran for 3,242 performances and won nine Tony Awards. A 1971 film adaptation followed.

Cuban revolutionary and politician; leader of [[Cuba]] from 1959 to 2011.

He was prime minister from 1959 to 1976, president from 1976 to 2008 and first secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba from 1965 until 2011. He took a key role in the [[Cuban Revolution]] by leading a guerrilla war against Fulgencio Batista from the Sierra Maestra. After Batista's overthrow in 1959, Cuba became a one-party communist state in which industry and business were nationalized.

Castro aligned Cuba with the [[Soviet Union]], which placed nuclear weapons in Cuba, resulting in the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]] of 1962. After the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991, Cuba entered an economic downturn known as the "Special Period." In 2006 he transferred his responsibilities to his brother [[Raúl Castro]].

He was the longest-serving non-royal head of state of the 20th and 21st centuries. Supporters credit his government with securing Cuba's independence from American hegemony. Critics argue that his administration oversaw human rights abuses and the exodus of many Cubans, and that it impoverished the economy.

Fast-paced team sport in which two teams of eleven players use curved sticks to drive a small, hard ball into the opponent's goal.

Matches are played on grass, turf or artificial turf, and indoor hockey is played on hard courts. Sticks, once wooden, are now usually made of carbon fiber, fiberglass and aramid. Only the flat face of the stick may move the ball, and only goalkeepers may touch it with their bodies inside the shooting circle. The modern game was developed at public schools in 19th-century England, and the International Hockey Federation (FIH) governs it.

Similar stick-and-ball games appear in the art of [[Ancient Egypt]] and [[Ancient Greece]]. In Sweden and Finland the sport is called landhockey and maahockey, meaning "ground" hockey, in contrast to [[Ice hockey]].

[[Algebraic structure]] with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division that behave as they do for rational numbers.

The best-known fields are the rational numbers, the real numbers and the complex numbers. Finite fields are used in [[Coding theory|error correction codes]] and [[Cryptography]], while number fields are studied in depth in [[Number theory]]. Field theory is a crucial ingredient in proofs that angle trisection and squaring the circle cannot be done with compass and straightedge alone. [[Galois theory]] provides an elegant proof of the Abel–Ruffini theorem that general quintic equations cannot be solved in radicals.

Any field may serve as the scalars of a [[Vector space]], the standard setting of linear algebra. Even more succinctly, a field is a [[Commutative ring|commutative ring]] in which 0 ≠ 1 and all nonzero elements are invertible under multiplication.

Physical quantity, represented by a scalar, vector, spinor or tensor, that has a value at each point in space and time.

A weather map of surface temperatures is a scalar field, and a map of wind speed and direction is a vector field. Field theories describe how field values change in space and time and are central to physics; electrodynamics can be formulated with two interacting vector fields or as a single rank-2 tensor field. In [[Quantum field theory]], a field occupies space and contains energy, which precludes a classical "true vacuum." The strength of most fields diminishes with distance; the gravitational and electrostatic fields of classical physics follow Gauss's law.

The field concept developed gradually. In the 18th century the gravitational field was devised to simplify the bookkeeping of forces under [[Isaac Newton]]'s law of universal gravitation. The independent concept of a field developed in the 19th century with electromagnetism, largely through the work of Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell.

Configurable [[Integrated circuit]] that can be repeatedly programmed after manufacturing.

An FPGA is a type of programmable logic device, consisting of a grid of logic blocks that can be configured in the field to interconnect and perform digital functions. It is often used for low-volume custom products and in research, and in [[Telecommunications]], automotive, aerospace and industrial systems. Designs are usually written in a hardware description language such as VHDL. The first commercially viable FPGA was produced by Xilinx, now owned by [[AMD]], in 1985.

Collection of raw data outside a laboratory, library or workplace setting.

Methods vary by discipline. Biologists may observe animals in their environments, while social scientists may interview or observe people to learn their languages, folklore and social structures. Common methods include informal interviews, direct observation, participation in the life of the group and life-histories; the approach is usually qualitative but often has quantitative dimensions. [[Anthropology]] has long relied on it, and [[Bronisław Malinowski]] and Alfred Radcliffe-Brown were early anthropologists who set the models for later work. Ethologists such as [[Jane Goodall]] also conduct field research.

Researchers keep detailed field notes and must try to avoid [[Ethnocentrism]], the belief in the superiority of one's own ethnic group. Participant observation, data collection and survey research are contrasted with experimental or laboratory research.

Award for two, three or four mathematicians under 40 years of age at each International Congress of Mathematicians, held every four years.

Often called the "Nobel Prize of Mathematics," it is named for Canadian mathematician John Charles Fields, who designed the medal and died before it was established. It was first awarded in 1936 at [[Oslo]] to Lars Ahlfors and Jesse Douglas. In 2014 [[Iran|Iranian]] mathematician Maryam Mirzakhani became the first woman to receive it. As of 2026, 68 people have been awarded the medal.

Edible [[Fruit|fruit]] of *Ficus carica*, a deciduous [[Tree|tree]] or large shrub in the flowering plant family [[Moraceae]], native to the Mediterranean region and to western and southern Asia.

The fruit develops as a teardrop-shaped syconium, 3–5 cm long, that ripens from green toward purple or brown and contains numerous small seeds. Its milky sap irritates human skin, but the figs can be eaten fresh or dried or processed into jam and other desserts. Because ripe figs are easily damaged in transport, most commercial production is dried or processed.

In 2020 world production of raw figs was 1.26 million tonnes. [[Turkey]] led with 25% of the world total, followed by [[Egypt]], [[Morocco]] and [[Algeria]], which together accounted for 62%. Raw figs contain roughly 80% water and 20% [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], with negligible protein or fat.

1999 American film directed by [[David Fincher]] and based on the 1996 novel *Fight Club* by Chuck Palahniuk.

Starring [[Brad Pitt]] and Edward Norton, it follows an insomniac office worker who forms an underground fight club with a soap salesman, Tyler Durden. Released in the United States on October 15, 1999, it fell short of studio expectations at the box office and polarized critics. It later became a cult classic on home video, and in 2009 *The New York Times* called it the "defining cult movie of our time."

Manned military aircraft designed primarily for air-to-air combat.

Fighters establish air superiority, which allows [[Bomber|bombers]] and [[Attack aircraft|attack aircraft]] to strike enemy targets. Many modern fighters also have ground-attack capabilities, and fighter-bombers are designed for both roles. Key performance features are firepower, high speed and maneuverability relative to the target aircraft.

Fighters first appeared in [[World War I]], when they were small, lightly armed biplanes with a top speed of about 100 mph (160 km/h). By [[World War II]] most were all-metal monoplanes armed with [[Machine gun|machine guns]] or cannon, and some approached 400 mph (640 km/h). Radar-homing missiles in the 1950s let fighters engage from any direction and at longer range. Air-to-air missiles largely replaced guns in the early 1960s, but the [[Vietnam War]] showed that guns still had a role, and most fighters built since then carry cannon as well as missiles.

Sport in which individuals, pairs or groups perform jumps, spins and dance moves on ice, wearing figure skates.

Figure skates differ from [[Ice hockey]] skates in having toe picks, which are used mainly for jumping. Figure skating was the first winter sport included in the [[Olympic Games]], at the 1908 Olympics in London. The Olympic disciplines are men's singles, women's singles, pair skating and ice dance; a team event was first included in the Winter Olympics in 2014. Senior skaters generally perform a short program and a free skate. The International Skating Union (ISU) regulates international judging and competition, and major competitions end with exhibition galas.

Archipelagic country in [[Melanesia]], [[Oceania]], in the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]], about 2,000 km (1,300 mi) north-northeast of [[New Zealand]].

Fiji consists of more than 330 islands, about 110 of them permanently inhabited, with a land area of about 18,300 sq km (7,100 sq mi). About 87% of the population live on the two major islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu. Most of the islands were formed by volcanic activity starting around 150 million years ago.

Austronesians settled the islands in the second millennium BC, followed by Melanesians. Britain established the Colony of Fiji in 1874, and the country became independent in 1970. After a series of coups, it became a republic in 1987, and Commodore Frank Bainimarama seized power in a 2006 coup. Bainimarama's FijiFirst party won 59.2% of the vote in the 2014 election, which international observers deemed credible. The economy is based mainly on [[Tourism|tourism]], with sugar cane, remittances and bottled water exports also important.

Method of organizing and accessing files on storage, provided locally by an [[Operating system|operating system]] or as a protocol between networked computers.

A file system lets applications share mass storage. Without one, applications could access storage in incompatible ways that cause resource contention, data corruption and data loss. File systems exist for [[Hard disk drive|hard disk drives]], [[Solid-state drive|solid-state drives]], [[Magnetic tape|magnetic tapes]] and [[Optical disc|optical discs]], and a portion of main memory can be set up as a RAM disk. File names are usually unique within a directory, most systems limit name length, and most modern systems accept a wide range of [[Unicode]] characters.

A local file system is typically layered. A logical layer offers an [[API]] for operations such as open, close, read and write, while a physical layer handles low-level access to the storage device.

Italian architect, designer, goldsmith and sculptor, considered a founding father of [[Renaissance architecture]].

Born in [[Florence]], he trained as a goldsmith and in 1401 competed for the Florence Baptistry doors against Lorenzo Ghiberti. He later devoted his attention to architecture and optics. He is most famous for designing the dome of the [[Florence Cathedral]], built without temporary scaffolding, and for developing the mathematical technique of linear [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], which governed pictorial depictions of space until the late 19th century.

In 1421 he became the first person to receive a patent in the Western world. Recognized as the first modern engineer, planner and sole construction supervisor, he also worked on sculpture, mathematics, engineering and ship design. Most of his surviving works are in Florence.

Facility that sells fuel and engine lubricants for motor vehicles.

Known as a gas station in the United States and Canada and as a petrol station in the United Kingdom and Australia, a filling station receives fuel from refineries by tank truck, stores it in typically underground tanks and sells it to motorists at a daily varied price. Fuel dispensers pump the fuel and calculate the amount due. The most common products are [[Gasoline|gasoline]] and [[Diesel fuel|diesel fuel]], along with liquefied petroleum gas, kerosene and alcohol fuels such as [[Methanol|methanol]] and [[Ethanol|ethanol]].

Many stations have convenience stores selling food, beverages, tobacco products, [[Lottery|lottery]] tickets, [[Newspaper|newspapers]] and [[Magazine|magazines]]. The first filling station in the modern sense opened in 1905 in [[St. Louis]], Missouri.

Organized, usually annual presentation of [[Film|films]], typically in one or more cinemas in a single city or region.

Festivals may be competitive or non-competitive, and many focus on a format such as documentary, a runtime such as short films, a genre such as [[Horror film|horror]], or a category of filmmakers. They are often regarded as launchpads for new filmmakers and independent films. The Venice Film Festival, begun in 1932, is the oldest still running. The most prestigious, known as the Big Five, are Venice, Cannes, Berlin, Toronto and Sundance, listed by date of foundation.

The [[San Francisco]] International Film Festival, held in March 1957, emphasized feature-length dramatic films and introduced foreign films to American audiences. Its first year included *Throne of Blood* by [[Akira Kurosawa]] and *Pather Panchali* by [[Satyajit Ray]].

Technological and commercial institutions of [[Filmmaking|filmmaking]], including production companies, studios, film festivals, distribution and actors.

Production concentrated under standing production companies, though cheaper equipment and outside investment have allowed independent production to grow. The worldwide theatrical market had a box office of US$42.2 billion in 2019, and the global box office declined to US$33.5 billion in 2025. Hollywood is the world's oldest national film industry and the largest by box office gross, while the [[Cinema of India|cinema of India]] leads in feature films produced and in ticket sales.

Significant centers of production in [[Europe]] are [[France]], [[Germany]] and [[Italy]], among others. The [[Cinema of China|cinema of China]] was introduced in 1896, and China became the second-largest market by box office receipts in 2012. The [[United States]] was among the countries with the largest number of film productions as of 2019.

Process of creating a motion picture, such as a feature film, streaming series, commercial, animation, music video or documentary.

Filmmaking is generally nonlinear: scripts are shot out of sequence, shots are repeated as needed, and footage is assembled in editing. A production typically has five stages. Development explores the idea, may secure rights to [[Intellectual property|intellectual property]], and obtains financing. Pre-production arranges the shoot, including hiring cast and crew, scouting locations and constructing sets. Production records the raw footage, and post-production edits it, mixes sound, adds visual effects and composes a score. Distribution releases the finished film to cinemas, home video or streaming services.

Films were originally recorded on [[Photographic film|photographic film]], but most filmmaking is now digital. Affordable digital technology has made independent filmmaking more accessible.

Device or process that removes unwanted components or features from a [[Signal processing|signal]].

Most often this means suppressing certain [[Frequency|frequencies]] or frequency bands, though in image processing filters may act on other targets. Filters are widely used in [[Electronics]], [[Telecommunications]], [[Radio|radio]], [[Television|television]], [[Radar|radar]], control systems and [[Computer graphics]].

Common linear filter families include the Chebyshev filter, the best approximation to an ideal response for a given order and ripple; the Butterworth filter, with a maximally flat passband response; the Bessel filter, with a maximally flat phase delay; and the elliptic filter, with the steepest cutoff. Bandforms include low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop and notch filters. Digital filters are classed as finite impulse response (FIR) or infinite impulse response (IIR).

Physical separation process in which a filter medium lets only the fluid pass, separating solid matter from it.

Solid particles that cannot pass through the medium are called oversize, and the fluid that passes is the filtrate. Oversize particles may form a filter cake on top of the filter or block its lattice, a condition called blinding. The largest particle that can pass defines the filter's effective pore size. Separation is imperfect, since solids retain some fluid and the filtrate may contain fine particles. Filtration is widely used in [[Chemical engineering]], and it occurs in nature too, in systems such as slow sand filters and filter feeders such as the [[Basking shark]].

Filtration differs from sieving, in which separation occurs at a single perforated layer, whereas a filter's multilayer lattice retains particles that cannot follow its tortuous channels. In everyday usage the verb "strain" is more common, as when draining cooking water from [[Pasta|pasta]] with a colander.

Japanese science fantasy media franchise created by Hironobu Sakaguchi and published by Square Enix.

The franchise centers on fantasy role-playing video games, though it has branched into action role-playing, third-person shooter and rhythm games. Its entries are mostly standalone stories with different settings and characters, linked by recurring mechanics and character names. The first game was released in Japan on December 18, 1987, and the franchise has expanded to sixteen main games, along with spin-offs and films, [[Anime|anime]], [[Manga|manga]] and novels. The series has sold more than 200 million copies worldwide.

[[Final Fantasy VII]] (1997) moved from two-dimensional to three-dimensional graphics on the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]], with polygonal characters on pre-rendered backgrounds. Music by Nobuo Uematsu is among the series' best-known features.
